tasks.prompt:
Support has collected these reports about issue discussions:

1. In a workspace of about 130 people, @-mentions of its longest-standing members stopped working some time ago. The name is highlighted in the text, but the person is not listed as mentioned and gets no alert. Mentioning people who joined recently works.
2. Read-only members never get mention alerts.
3. When someone is @-mentioned in a comment on an issue they are assigned to, they get two alerts for that one comment.
4. A reply to a reply is counted in the issue's comment count but does not appear in the thread.
5. When a comment is deleted, the replies beneath it disappear as well.
6. Editing a comment to add a mention does not alert the newly mentioned person, the comment keeps listing the old mentions, and searching for the new wording does not find it.
7. The fifteen-minute edit limit only holds for comments that were never edited: people who edit once within the window keep editing for days.
8. Nobody is told when someone replies to their comment.
9. When one teammate pastes a flood of comments, nobody else in the workspace can comment for a while.

Expected behaviour:

- Mentions. Anyone who is currently an active member of the workspace can be mentioned by their handle — the part of their email address before the @, matched case-insensitively — whatever their role and however many members the workspace has. A handle shared by several members mentions all of them. The members recorded as mentioned on a comment, and alerted, are exactly those its text mentions (outside code), except the comment's author, whose own handle is ignored. Members of other workspaces are never mentioned, whatever their handle.
- Alerts. When a comment is posted, the issue's author, its current assignee and — for a reply — the author of the comment being answered are told that a comment was added, and the people the comment mentions are told that they were mentioned. Each person gets at most one alert for one comment, and a mention alert takes precedence over a comment alert. The comment's author gets nothing. Each recipient's notification preferences apply as for any other alert.
- The thread. A reply may answer a reply. The thread of an issue lists its top-level comments oldest first and, under each one, every reply that descends from it — directly or through other replies — in order of posting, however deep the chain. A deleted comment keeps its place as a placeholder, marked as deleted and without its text, so the replies under it stay where they were. The issue's comment count is the number of its comments that are not deleted.
- Edits. The author of a comment may edit it within fifteen minutes of posting it; the limit is counted from the original posting, never from an edit. Whoever the permission rules allow to edit other people's comments is not bound by it. An edit re-reads the mentions from the new text: the recorded mentions become exactly what the new text mentions, people newly mentioned are alerted once, people who were already mentioned are not alerted again, and the edited text is what search finds.
- The posting limit applies per member: one member's burst is charged to that member alone and never stops anyone else from commenting.

tasks.prompt:
Reports from support and security about alerts and the inbox:

1. Security: any member can open another member's inbox by changing the address, and can mark another member's alerts as read. Changing another member's notification settings works too.
2. "Mark all read" in one person's inbox clears the unread alerts of everyone else in the workspace.
3. Clicking an alert about an issue opens a page that does not exist. The links in search results and in the daily digest are broken the same way, and the alert about a new member leads nowhere either.
4. Since a recent change, owners are no longer told when someone joins the workspace; the person who joined gets an alert about themselves instead.
5. Assignees are not told when someone else moves their issue to another status, on the board or otherwise.
6. Someone assigned at the moment an issue is created gets no assignment alert; they only get one when assigned later.
7. When the workspace runs out of room on its plan — a project, a seat, an issue, an upload or a webhook endpoint refused — the owner never hears about it.
8. Alerts a member switched off for the inbox still show up there.

Expected behaviour:

- Inboxes and notification settings are personal: a member reads, marks read and configures only their own, whatever their role; anyone else's are refused. Marking all read marks that member's own unread alerts and nothing else. An inbox lists exactly the alerts delivered to it in-app, however many, with no entry duplicated or missing across pages; an alert the member switched off for in-app never appears there, whatever other channels it goes to.
- Every alert and every search hit links to the page the app actually serves. An alert about an issue (assignment, status change, overdue reminder, comment, mention), a search hit for an issue and a search hit for a comment all link to that issue's page in its workspace and project; a search hit for a project links to the project's page; the alert about a new member links to the members settings page; the alert about a full plan links to the billing settings page. Digest entries carry the same links as the alerts they summarise.
- The workspace owner is told when a new member joins; the person who joined is not told about themselves.
- The assignee of an issue is told when somebody else changes its status, including by moving it on the board; nobody is told about their own change, and nothing is sent for an issue that has no assignee. Being assigned at creation is an assignment: the assignee is told exactly as if assigned later, unless they created the issue themselves.
- When a write is refused because the plan has no room for it — another project, another seat (an invitation), another issue in a project, another upload, another webhook endpoint — the workspace owner is told, whoever tried. While that alert is still unread, further refusals for the same resource add nothing; once it has been read, the next refusal produces a new alert. Refusals for different resources are separate alerts. The periodic usage recount, which refuses nothing, never produces one.

tasks.prompt:
Support has these reports about projects:

1. A workspace on the Free plan archived one of its two projects and still cannot create another: "the plan allows 2 projects".
2. Creating a project whose name begins like an existing one — "Web Visitors" next to "Web Vendors" — fails with "Something went wrong". The same happens when the look-alike project was archived long ago.
3. A new project was given the address of an archived project without complaint. Restoring the archived one afterwards fails with "Something went wrong".
4. Restoring an archived project let a Free workspace run three projects at once, and the projects meter on the billing page kept showing two until the periodic recount.
5. Restoring a project from a stale tab, when the project was not archived at all, reported success and left a "restored" entry behind.
6. Pausing or completing a project on its settings page looks saved, but the project is still shown as active afterwards and still accepts new issues. A project can be marked completed while it still has open issues.

Expected behaviour:

- Keys and addresses. Every project in a workspace has its own key, archived projects included — their issue numbers still carry it. When the key a project would get (chosen, or derived from the name) is already in use, it is made unique the way the address is: by appending a number, trimmed so the key never exceeds four characters. The address of an archived project stays reserved, so a new project asking for it gets a different one and the archived project can be restored under its own. Keys and addresses are per workspace.
- Plan slots. Only live projects count against the plan's project limit: archiving a project frees its slot at once and restoring it takes a slot again. Restoring is refused when the plan has no room for another project, and nothing is restored or announced. The workspace's projects meter follows immediately — after a restore it shows one more, and the periodic recount agrees with it — through any sequence of archiving and restoring.
- Restoring. Only an archived project can be restored; restoring one that is not archived is refused and announces nothing. A restored project comes back exactly as it was, with the status it had, and its archived issues stay archived.
- Status. A project is active, paused or completed; the status that is saved is the status the project has, and the project list's status filter reports it. New issues can be created only in an active project: a paused or completed project refuses them, nothing is created and nothing is announced, while its existing issues can still be worked on (status changes, comments) as before. A project can be marked completed only when none of its issues is open — done and canceled issues and archived issues are not open — however many issues it has; otherwise the request is refused and the project stays as it was. Marking it paused is always possible, and so is reactivating it. Marking a completed project completed again changes nothing. An archived project's status cannot be changed, and changing a status takes the same right as editing the project.

tasks.prompt:
Product change: paid subscriptions renew period by period and are invoiced.

Today a subscription records a plan, a billing interval, a seat count and a current period, and nothing ever moves the period on or writes an invoice. From now on a background job renews subscriptions whose period has ended, every renewed paid period is invoiced, cancellations take effect on their date, and changes made in the middle of a period are charged for the rest of it.

Periods

- A period is the span from its start up to its end. A monthly period ends on the same day of the following month at the same time of day — or on that month's last day when it has no such day (31 January → 28 February); an annual period ends on the same day and month of the following year (29 February → 28 February). Each new period starts exactly where the previous one ended, so a clamped day carries forward (28 February → 28 March).
- The full charge for one period is the plan's monthly price per seat (`priceCentsPerSeatMonthly` in `src/config/plan-limits.ts`) × the subscription's seats × the months in the period (1 monthly, 12 annual), in cents.

The renewal job

- `src/server/jobs/billing-renewal-job.ts`: `export async function runBillingRenewalJob(now: Date): Promise<JobResult>`, a job like the existing ones (job kind `billing-renewal`, scheduled hourly, with a cron trigger route like the other jobs have). It looks at every workspace's subscription, however many workspaces there are, skipping deleted (archived) workspaces entirely.
- An `active` subscription whose period end lies at or before `now` is renewed: one new period per elapsed interval, until its period end lies after `now` (a subscription three months behind gets three consecutive periods). Each new period of a paid plan is invoiced for the full charge of that period, at the seat count at that moment. The free plan's periods move on the same way, without invoices.
- A `canceled` subscription whose cancellation date lies at or before `now` ends: the workspace moves to the free plan as of the cancellation date — plan `free`, status `active`, no cancellation pending, a new monthly period starting at the cancellation date — and `billing.plan_changed` is published once (from the paid plan to `free`, no actor). No invoice. Before the cancellation date nothing happens, whatever the period end says.
- `trialing` and `past_due` subscriptions are left alone by this job (the trial-expiry job keeps its role).
- The job is replay-safe: running it again at the same instant changes nothing — no second invoice, no second period, no second announcement.

Invoices

- An invoice carries the workspace, a number unique within the workspace, the amount in cents, currency `usd`, the period it covers (start and end), and no payment date. They are listed through the existing `listInvoices`, newest period first.
- Every invoice is published once as `billing.invoice_issued` (`EventEnvelope & { invoiceId: string; invoiceNumber: string; amountCents: number; periodStart: IsoTimestamp; periodEnd: IsoTimestamp }`, added to `TaskflowEventMap`), recorded once in the audit log as the action `billing.invoice_issued` (subject kind `subscription`, subject id = the workspace id), and the workspace owner is told once about it with a new notification kind `invoice_issued` — accepted everywhere the existing kinds are, including the zod schemas that validate audit-log filters and notification-preference updates. Nobody else is told.

Mid-period changes (`updateSeats`, `changePlan`)

- Proration: a change made in the middle of a period is charged the full-period amount of the change, scaled by the days left over the days in the period, rounded down to whole cents. Days left are counted as whole or started days from the moment of the change to the period end (14 days and 22 hours left count as 15); there are none once the period end has been reached. The days in the period are the whole days between its start and its end (rounded, at least one). A charge of zero cents produces no invoice. A prorated invoice covers the current period and is issued, published, audited and announced like a renewal invoice; the period itself is unchanged.
- Adding seats to a paid, active subscription is charged for the seats added (the plan's monthly price × seats added × months in the period, prorated). Removing seats charges and credits nothing. Seat changes on the free plan or during a trial charge nothing.
- Changing the plan: moving between two paid plans while active charges the price difference per seat (if positive) × seats × months in the period, prorated; a downgrade or an unchanged plan charges nothing, and the period is unchanged. Choosing a plan during a trial charges nothing and keeps the trial period (the first invoice comes when it ends). Leaving the free plan for a paid one starts a fresh period at that moment, with the chosen interval, invoiced in full. Moving to the free plan charges nothing.
- Everything else about these two operations — permissions, the seat ceiling, the downgrade refusal — is unchanged.

"Now" is the moment of the call (the `now` handed to the job).

Invoices are persisted in the existing invoices table; a freshly migrated database (the way the test suite builds one) must work as is.

Update any visible test that encodes behaviour this change alters.

tasks.prompt:
Product change: issues get sub-issues.

An issue already records a parent id, but nothing gives it meaning. From now on an issue may sit under a parent issue of its own project, trees stay shallow and never loop, the work below an issue can be listed and counted, archiving takes the sub-issues along, and the person responsible for an issue hears when its last open sub-issue is closed.

User stories

- As someone who may edit an issue, I can put it under a parent issue — when I create it or at any later time — move it under another parent, or make it a root issue again. The sub-issues below it move with it.
- As someone who may read an issue, I can list its direct sub-issues and see a roll-up of everything below it.
- As the assignee of an issue with sub-issues, I am told once when its last open sub-issue is closed.

Rules

- Guards, in the spirit of the other issue operations: an `orgId` outside the actor's workspace → `TenantScopeError`, on every operation. An issue that does not exist in that workspace (including another workspace's) → `NotFoundError` (the one in `src/server/services/_support.ts`). Placing or moving an issue takes `issue:update` on that issue (the existing escalation for one's own issue applies); listing sub-issues and reading the roll-up take `issue:read` on the issue. An archived issue cannot be moved (`AlreadyArchivedError`).
- The parent must be a live issue of the same project: an issue of another project or another workspace → `NotFoundError`; an archived issue → `AlreadyArchivedError`. The same applies to a parent given at creation; a refused creation creates nothing and announces nothing.
- The tree never loops: an issue cannot be placed under itself or under anything below it → `IssueHierarchyError` with reason `"cycle"`.
- Depth: a root issue is at level 0 and nothing may sit deeper than level `MAX_SUB_ISSUE_DEPTH` (add `export const MAX_SUB_ISSUE_DEPTH: number = 3` to `src/config/constants.ts`). Because the sub-issues below an issue move with it, a move is judged by where its deepest descendant would land → `IssueHierarchyError` with reason `"too_deep"`. A refused move changes nothing.
- `IssueHierarchyError` (new, `src/lib/issue-hierarchy.ts`): `export class IssueHierarchyError extends Error` with `readonly code = "conflict"`, `readonly issueId: string` and `readonly reason: "cycle" | "too_deep"`; `toAppError` maps it to `conflict` and `isDomainError` recognises it.
- A successful move or removal of a parent is announced as the existing `issue.updated` event with `changedFields: ["parentId"]`.
- Listing: the direct sub-issues that are not archived, oldest first (creation time, then issue number).
- Roll-up: counts over every issue below the issue at any depth that is not archived — `total`, `open` and `closed`, closed meaning done or canceled — however many there are.
- Archiving an issue archives every live issue below it, at any depth, with it; issues already archived stay exactly as they were. Each issue archived this way is announced with its own `issue.archived` event, exactly once, so everything that follows an archive today (the issues counter, the search index, alerts) follows for all of them. Archiving a sub-issue never touches its parent.
- Completion notice: when a sub-issue stops being open — its status changes from an open status to done or canceled, or it is archived while open — and its direct parent is left with no open issue below it (at any depth), the parent's assignee is told once with a new notification kind `sub_issues_completed`, accepted everywhere the existing kinds are, including the zod schema that validates notification-preference updates. It goes through the usual fan-out, so the recipient's preferences apply and the person who made the change is never told about their own. Nothing is sent when the parent has no assignee or is archived, when the change is not a closing (moving a sub-issue away, reopening one, a closed issue changing to another closed status), or for a parent without sub-issues. Reopening a sub-issue and closing it again tells the assignee again. Only the direct parent is considered.

"Now" is the moment of the call. Nothing new needs to be persisted beyond the existing issues table.

API — add these exports:

In `src/types/issue.ts`:

```ts
export interface IssueRollup {
  readonly total: number;
  readonly open: number;
  readonly closed: number;
}
```

In `src/schemas/issue.ts`:

```ts
export const setIssueParentSchema = z.object({
  orgId: orgIdSchema,
  issueId: issueIdSchema,
  parentId: issueIdSchema.nullable(),
});
export type SetIssueParentInput = z.infer<typeof setIssueParentSchema>;
```

In `src/server/services/issue-service.ts`:

- `export async function setIssueParent(actor: Actor, input: SetIssueParentInput): Promise<Issue>` — resolves to the issue as stored afterwards.
- `export async function listSubIssues(actor: Actor, orgId: OrgId, issueId: IssueId): Promise<readonly Issue[]>`
- `export async function getIssueRollup(actor: Actor, orgId: OrgId, issueId: IssueId): Promise<IssueRollup>`

Update any visible test that encodes behaviour this change alters.

tasks.notes: Implement (product spec, no bug.patch): sub-issue hierarchy on the dormant parent_id column — parent placement at creation or later with same-project/live validation, cycle and depth rules judged on the subtree that moves, direct-children listing, a roll-up over every live descendant, an archive cascade that announces each archived issue once, and a completion notice to the parent's assignee when its last open sub-issue closes. Reference solution: 12 files, 386 changed lines across config (MAX_SUB_ISSUE_DEPTH), lib/issue-hierarchy (IssueHierarchyError, fitsDepth), lib/errors, types (IssueRollup, notification kind), zod (setIssueParentSchema, notification kind), the drizzle notification-kind enum, issue-repository (setIssueParent, listChildIssues, listDescendants as a level-by-level inArray walk with no page cap, countDescendants, depthOf, archiveIssues as one UPDATE … RETURNING), issue-service (requireUsableParent shared by createIssue and setIssueParent; subtree height from listDescendants; archiveIssue cascades and emits one issue.archived per descendant), notification-service (issue.status_changed open→closed and issue.archived-while-open subscribers that look at the direct parent's roll-up and notify through notify(), so preferences and the actor exclusion apply) and the UI label record. Why hard: the parent rule has two entry points (creation and move); the depth rule must account for the subtree that moves, which the obvious "parent depth + 1" ignores; descendants must be walked without a page cap (the issue list caps at 100); the cascade must announce every archived issue so the usage counter and the search index stay honest, which a single event does not; and the completion notice is a transition (open → not open) on the direct parent, not a state (zero open), so a move or a reopen must not fire it. Traps: scale (naive B, descendants read 100 per level: fails the 150-children roll-up); wrong place (naive C, the parent validated on a later move only: fails the creation refusals and the depth case); second cause (naive D, the cascade archives the descendants but announces only the root: fails the cascade case, where the counter and the events are checked); boundary (naive E, the depth check ignores the moving subtree: fails the depth case); ordering/second cause (naive F, the notice also fires when a move leaves the parent with nothing open: fails "a closing, not a rearrangement").
